cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: ABI3 encodes a B3-domain transcription factor that is a master regulator of seed maturation, dormancy, and desiccation tolerance in plants, while its mammalian ortholog NESH/ABI3 functions as an SH3-domain adaptor in actin cytoskeleton remodeling and cell migration. In plants, ABI3 directly binds RY/Sph (CATGCA) motifs via its B3 domain and activates ABA-responsive elements (ABREs) via its B2 domain to control seed storage protein genes, chlorophyll degradation, and stress-response programs; it acts upstream of ABI5 in ABA signaling, autoregulates its own expression through chromatin remodeling, participates in reciprocal regulatory loops with ERF1 to modulate auxin/ABA crosstalk, and represses JAZ1 via H3K27me3-mediated silencing to control root elongation [PMID:11029704, PMID:12410810, PMID:30019436, PMID:37450369, PMID:39495594]. ABI3 protein stability is controlled by AIP2 RING E3 ligase-mediated polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation [PMID:15998807]. In mammals, NESH/ABI3 incorporates into the WAVE regulatory complex where it displaces Abi-1, suppresses lamellipodia formation and cell migration, binds F-actin in dendritic spines to regulate synapse morphogenesis, and supports microglial phagocytosis and amyloid-β clearance—loss of Abi3 in a 5XFAD mouse model increases amyloid plaque burden, linking ABI3 to Alzheimer's disease risk [PMID:26428302, PMID:22485184, PMID:34731000].

AIFM1 encodes a bifunctional mitochondrial FAD-dependent flavoprotein that serves as an NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (NDH-2) essential for respiratory chain complex I biogenesis and, upon apoptotic or necrotic stimuli, acts as a caspase-independent cell death effector [PMID:10381654, PMID:26063804, PMID:20138767]. In healthy cells, AIFM1 is anchored to the inner mitochondrial membrane where its physical interaction with CHCHD4 (MIA40) facilitates import of electron transport chain subunits into the intermembrane space; SIRT5-dependent desuccinylation maintains this interaction [PMID:26004228, PMID:36653443]. Upon death signals—including PARP-1–generated PAR polymer, calpain-mediated cleavage, or GPX4 inactivation—truncated AIF is released to the cytosol; in the nucleus it binds γH2AX via its C-terminal proline-rich domain and recruits cyclophilin A to form a DNA-degrading complex executing parthanatos, while HSP70 and thioredoxin-1 oppose this translocation [PMID:20360685, PMID:22972376, PMID:15941767, PMID:19332058, PMID:12022952, PMID:26119781]. Pathogenic AIFM1 variants (e.g., G308E) impair FAD-dependent redox activity and mitochondrial respiration, causing X-linked mitochondrial encephalomyopathy [PMID:27178839].

ATP6AP1 (Ac45) is an accessory subunit of the V0 sector of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase that functions as a V-ATPase assembly factor, trafficking guide, and signaling integrator at endomembranes. Synthesized as an N-glycosylated precursor, it undergoes furin-mediated proteolytic cleavage in the secretory pathway; the processed C-terminal form directs V-ATPase through the secretory pathway to regulate organellar and extracellular acidification, Ca²⁺-dependent exocytosis in neuroendocrine cells, and lysosomal trafficking via Rab7 interaction in osteoclasts [PMID:18713856, PMID:20702583, PMID:22736765, PMID:22467241]. ATP6AP1 additionally acts as an unconventional guanine nucleotide exchange factor for Rheb, coupling V-ATPase-associated lysosomal signaling to mTORC1 activation through a conserved tri-aspartate motif in its cytoplasmic tail [PMID:38448650]. Hemizygous missense mutations in ATP6AP1 cause an X-linked syndrome of immunodeficiency with hypogammaglobulinemia, hepatopathy, and neurocognitive abnormalities, while somatic inactivating mutations drive granular cell tumor oncogenesis [PMID:27231034, PMID:30166553].

SPRING1 (C12ORF49/POST1) is a glycosylated Golgi-resident membrane protein that functions as an essential cofactor for site-1 protease (S1P/MBTPS1) maturation, binding S1P via its conserved DUF2054 domain and promoting its autocatalytic processing from the precursor S1P-A and intermediate S1P-B'/B forms to the fully active S1P-C'/C form [PMID:32666500, PMID:32694732]. This S1P activation is required for proteolytic cleavage of multiple substrates including SREBP transcription factors, ATF6, CREB3 family members, and the α/β-subunit precursor of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, thereby controlling cholesterol and fatty acid homeostasis, the unfolded protein response, and lysosome biogenesis [PMID:32666500]. Loss of SPRING1 reduces SCAP protein levels and causes sterol-independent SCAP mislocalization to the Golgi, blocking SREBP signaling; this defect is rescued by SCAP re-expression, and hepatic silencing in mice or genetic ablation in zebrafish phenocopies S1P loss-of-function by impairing dietary lipid clearance [PMID:32111832, PMID:32694732].

CCDC30 encodes a coiled-coil domain-containing protein whose native cellular function remains largely uncharacterized. It has been identified as a fusion partner of ROS1 in papillary thyroid carcinoma, where the coiled-coil domain of CCDC30 is predicted to mediate ligand-independent dimerization and constitutive activation of the ROS1 kinase domain [PMID:27089969]. The resulting CCDC30::ROS1 fusion protein induces MAPK pathway phosphorylation and promotes cell proliferation, effects that are reversed by ROS1-specific inhibitors [PMID:39982551].

Cyclin C (CCNC) is the obligate activating subunit of CDK8 (and CDK19), forming a kinase complex that phosphorylates transcriptional regulators to control gene expression programs in development, metabolism, and stress responses. The CycC–CDK8 complex phosphorylates the Notch intracellular domain within its TAD and PEST domains, triggering Fbw7/Sel10-dependent ubiquitin-mediated degradation [PMID:15546612], and suppresses de novo lipogenesis by promoting turnover of nuclear SREBP-1c downstream of mTORC1 [PMID:26042770]. Structural studies show that CDK8 employs a unique CycC-recognition helix and an unphosphorylated activation loop, with full kinase activation requiring allosteric T-loop repositioning by Med12 or MTBP [PMID:21806996]. In vivo, CCNC is required for brown adipocyte progenitor proliferation via the C/EBPα/GLUT4/ChREBP axis [PMID:35863637] and for autophagy-lysosome pathway gene transcription in the pancreas, where its loss accelerates Kras-driven neoplasia [PMID:bio_10.1101_2024.08.21.609015].

CEP164 is a distal appendage protein of the mother centriole that serves as a master scaffold for ciliogenesis initiation, vesicle docking, and intraflagellar transport, while also participating in DNA damage signaling and Hedgehog pathway regulation. CEP164 homodimerizes via its central coiled-coil domain to anchor at the mother centriole and directly recruits the kinase TTBK2 through multivalent electrostatic interactions involving its intrinsically disordered region, forming phase-separated condensates that drive CP110 removal and IFT machinery assembly [PMID:24982133, PMID:40305080, PMID:40483689]. In multiciliated cells, CEP164 controls vesicle recruitment, ciliary vesicle formation, basal body docking, and recruitment of Chibby1, while in photoreceptors it is continuously required for IFT complex maintenance after initial cilium assembly [PMID:29244804, PMID:36074756]. CEP164 is phosphorylated at Ser186 by ATR/ATM and facilitates CHK1 activation in the DNA damage response, and independently scaffolds GLI2 at the centriole to regulate Hedgehog target gene expression [PMID:18283122, PMID:37199136].

CLPB encodes a AAA+ ATPase that functions as a protein disaggregase, with the bacterial ortholog ClpB operating as a hexameric ring that threads aggregated polypeptides through its central pore in ATP hydrolysis-driven steps, cooperating with the DnaK/DnaJ/GrpE chaperone system to solubilize and reactivate aggregated proteins [PMID:10497158, PMID:15550247, PMID:23393091]. Human CLPB (SKD3) localizes to mitochondria, where PARL-mediated removal of an autoinhibitory peptide activates its stand-alone disaggregase function; its unique ankyrin-repeat domain maintains higher-order oligomeric assembly (tetradecamers remodeling to dodecamers upon substrate engagement) and is essential for disaggregase activity [PMID:32573439, PMID:36745679]. Conserved pore-loop residues in both NBD1 and NBD2 form a spiral staircase that grips and translocates substrate polypeptides in two-amino-acid steps, while the middle domain acts as an autoinhibitory and DnaK-interaction element whose conformational switching regulates ring activation [PMID:30257943, PMID:31216466, PMID:24843029]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function CLPB mutations cause an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, cataracts, and neutropenia, and heterozygous dominant-negative missense variants near the ATP-binding pocket inhibit wild-type CLPB ATPase/disaggregase activity and impair granulopoiesis [PMID:25597511, PMID:34115842].

COX4I1 encodes the ubiquitous isoform 1 of subunit 4 of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), serving as a nuclear-encoded regulatory subunit essential for complex IV assembly, stability, and respiratory efficiency. Under normoxia COX4-1 is the predominant isoform; hypoxia triggers HIF-1-dependent transcriptional activation of COX4-2 and LON-mediated degradation of COX4-1, switching subunit composition to optimize ATP production and limit ROS [PMID:17418790]. COX4-1 promotes assembly of respiratory supercomplexes, and its complete loss abolishes complex IV, secondarily impairs complex I biogenesis and mitochondrial translation, causes replicative stress with defective DNA damage repair, and in cancer cells rewires redox metabolism to favor apoptosis over ferroptosis [PMID:33578848, PMID:35478774, PMID:35456968, PMID:41596099]. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in COX4I1 cause cytochrome c oxidase deficiency presenting as mitochondrial disease, confirmed by lentiviral rescue of enzymatic activity in patient fibroblasts [PMID:28766551].

COX4I2 is a tissue-specific isoform of the nuclear-encoded subunit IV of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) that modulates electron transport chain activity and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Its expression is transcriptionally regulated by HIF1A under hypoxia and by EBF1 in cancer-associated fibroblasts, post-translationally controlled by SIRT3-mediated deacetylation that maintains mitochondrial respiratory homeostasis, and post-transcriptionally suppressed by Rpl13a snoRNA U32A-guided 2′-O-methylation of its mRNA [PMID:19268275, PMID:38422899, PMID:39002521, PMID:36683245, PMID:40777413]. Through its regulation of COX activity and ROS levels, COX4I2 influences ferroptosis, apoptosis, and angiogenesis in cell-type-specific contexts: it promotes ROS-driven ferroptosis in Schwann cells via ERK signaling, drives fibroblast-mediated angiogenesis in pheochromocytoma, and when delivered by exosomes from cancer-associated fibroblasts suppresses ferroptosis in osteosarcoma cells [PMID:34026834, PMID:36172142, PMID:40977891]. Loss-of-function mutations in COX4I2 cause pancreatic acinic cell dysplasia with attenuated hypoxic COX4I2 induction [PMID:19268275].

COX7B is a nuclear-encoded, late-assembled structural subunit of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) that is essential for Complex IV assembly, enzymatic activity, and oxidative phosphorylation. Its assembly into Complex IV intermediates is interdependent with other late-assembled subunits, and its structural position is functionally conserved from protostome invertebrates to vertebrates despite sequence divergence [PMID:20307258, PMID:35699132]. Loss of COX7B causes microcephaly and microphthalmia in vertebrate models and underlies linear skin defects with multiple congenital anomalies (MLS/LSDMCA syndrome) in humans [PMID:23122588, PMID:42014911]. COX7B expression levels modulate reactive oxygen species production and downstream PPAR signaling in proliferative keratinocytes, cisplatin sensitivity in cancer cells, and cardiac function under hypertrophic stress [PMID:38855186, PMID:30367559, PMID:37979444].

CTR9 is the TPR-domain scaffold subunit of the PAF1 complex (PAF1C), functioning as a central organizer of RNA Polymerase II-coupled transcription elongation and co-transcriptional chromatin modification. Its TPR module heterodimerizes with PAF1 to nucleate PAF1C assembly, and disruption of this interface abolishes complex formation, histone H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 deposition, and yeast viability [PMID:30228257, PMID:11884586]. CTR9 restrains Polycomb-mediated H3K27me3 by maintaining PRC2 subtype equilibrium (PRC2.2 over PRC2.1), regulates NELF/SPT5-dependent elongation pausing at stimulus-responsive loci such as c-Fos, controls ERα stability and genome-wide ERα/RNAPII chromatin occupancy in estrogen signaling, and is itself targeted for proteasomal degradation via SIAH1-mediated K48-linked polyubiquitination [PMID:35137163, PMID:23593388, PMID:26494790, PMID:37038329]. De novo CTR9 missense variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder, with patient-derived mutations showing enhanced PAF1 binding affinity and dominant-negative effects in zebrafish [PMID:35717577].

CYP26A1 is a retinoic acid (RA)-catabolizing cytochrome P450 enzyme that shapes RA gradients during embryonic development and governs RA clearance in adult tissues. It hydroxylates all-trans-RA with high isomer specificity (Km ~50 nM) to 4-OH-RA, 4-oxo-RA, 16-OH-RA, and 18-OH-RA, and further metabolizes these products; it is the dominant RA-clearing enzyme in human liver and its catalytic efficiency is modulated by direct protein–protein interactions with CRABP1 and CRABP2 [PMID:22020119, PMID:20513361, PMID:35565751]. CYP26A1 transcription is auto-induced by RA through two synergistic RAREs in its promoter that bind pre-loaded RARγ/RXRα heterodimers, with co-regulation by Sp1/Sp3, WNT/β-catenin, and Polycomb-mediated bivalent chromatin [PMID:10976925, PMID:16053444, PMID:17663992, PMID:16885356]. Cyp26a1-null mice die in utero with spina bifida, caudal truncation, hindbrain mis-patterning, and homeotic vertebral transformations caused by unopposed RA signaling through a RARγ–WNT3A/FGF8 axis, and triple CYP26-family knockouts reveal axis duplication from expanded Nodal expression, establishing CYP26A1 as an essential architect of RA-depleted embryonic territories [PMID:11157778, PMID:12588859, PMID:19605690].

DIPK1A (formerly FAM69A) is computationally predicted to encode a protein kinase containing conserved catalytic phosphotransferase motifs and an EF-hand Ca²⁺-binding domain inserted within its kinase domain, suggesting a role as a Ca²⁺-dependent kinase acting on substrates in the secretory pathway [PMID:23840464]. Direct biochemical or cellular mechanistic characterization of the DIPK1A protein has not been reported.

DLD encodes dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3), the FAD-dependent oxidoreductase that catalyzes NAD⁺-dependent oxidation of dihydrolipoamide as the shared E3 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, and the glycine cleavage system, thereby occupying a central node in mitochondrial oxidative metabolism [PMID:28579060, PMID:2188967]. The α-KGDH complex containing DLD also translocates to the nucleus, where it associates with KAT2A to supply succinyl-CoA for histone H3 lysine 79 succinylation, linking DLD-dependent metabolism to epigenetic gene regulation and tumor cell proliferation [PMID:29211711]. DLD is specifically required for cystine deprivation-induced ferroptosis, functioning upstream of mitochondrial iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation through its regulation of α-KGDH activity [PMID:31931284]. Loss-of-function DLD mutations cause dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency—manifesting as lactic acidosis, Leigh syndrome, and multi-organ pathology—through impaired enzymatic activity, disrupted E2 binding, and enhanced ROS generation [PMID:28579060, PMID:23290025].

DPM2 is an 84-amino acid ER-resident membrane protein that serves as a regulatory subunit of the heterotrimeric dolichol-phosphate-mannose (DPM) synthase complex (DPM1/DPM2/DPM3), where it stabilizes DPM3, promotes ER retention of the catalytic DPM1 subunit, enhances dolichol phosphate substrate binding, and increases DPM synthase activity approximately 10-fold [PMID:9724629, PMID:10835346]. DPM2 additionally associates with and stimulates the GPI-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase complex through interactions with PIG-A, PIG-C, and GPI1, thereby co-regulating both dolichol-phosphate-mannose-dependent glycosylation and GPI anchor biosynthesis in the ER [PMID:10944123]. Loss-of-function mutations in DPM2 cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation with deficient N-glycosylation and O-mannosylation, manifesting as dystroglycanopathy [PMID:23109149].

DTL (also known as CDT2 or DCAF2) is the substrate-recognition subunit of the CRL4^CDT2 E3 ubiquitin ligase, serving as a central regulator of DNA replication licensing, DNA damage responses, and cell cycle checkpoints. DTL bridges the CUL4–DDB1 catalytic core to substrates bearing a PIP degron—a specialized PCNA-interaction motif containing TD and downstream basic residues—on chromatin-loaded PCNA, thereby directing ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation of CDT1, p21, SET8/PR-Set7, CHK1, XPG, FBH1, CRY1, PDCD4, DNA-PKcs, and RUVBL1 during S phase, after DNA damage, and in circadian regulation [PMID:16949367, PMID:20932472, PMID:21143559, PMID:23677613, PMID:26431207, PMID:31409387, PMID:33627782, PMID:38609375]. DTL binds PCNA directly through a high-affinity C-terminal PIP box (~100-fold greater than substrate PIP boxes), and its own abundance is tightly controlled by SCF^FBXO11-mediated degradation—antagonized by 14-3-3 binding to phospho-Thr464—and by CRL4^DDB2-dependent ubiquitylation [PMID:30623174, PMID:23478441, PMID:25154416, PMID:33557942]. Beyond replication control, DTL functions in a CDT1-independent G2/M checkpoint, regulates NIK-dependent IL-23 signaling in dendritic cells, and is essential for early embryonic development, with maternal DTL preventing DNA re-replication in the first zygotic cell cycle [PMID:17085480, PMID:30018073, PMID:28818995, PMID:17107960].
