cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: EIF2S3 encodes eIF2γ, the central GTPase subunit of the heterotrimeric eIF2 complex that delivers Met-tRNAiMet to the 40S ribosomal subunit during translation initiation. eIF2γ binds GTP and the acceptor stem of Met-tRNAi directly, while its domain III contacts 18S rRNA helix h44 on the ribosome rather than tRNA, distinguishing it functionally from the structurally related elongation factor EF-Tu [PMID:15788752, PMID:22002225]. The β subunit of eIF2 binds eIF2γ through a ~78-residue C-terminal region, and proper eIF2 heterotrimer assembly requires the dedicated assembly factor CDC123, which engages the unassembled γ subunit via its domain III [PMID:10769173, PMID:23775072]. Loss-of-function mutations in EIF2S3 cause MEHMO syndrome (intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypogonadism, microcephaly, obesity) by disrupting eIF2 complex integrity, reducing ternary complex levels, and dysregulating the integrated stress response—defects partially rescued by the eIF2B activator ISRIB [PMID:23063529, PMID:28055140, PMID:31836389].

EPOP is an accessory subunit of the PRC2.1 Polycomb repressive complex that tunes the balance between gene repression and low-level transcription at developmental loci, particularly Hox genes, in pluripotent and early differentiating cells. EPOP recruits Elongin BC and the deubiquitinase USP7 to bivalent and active chromatin via a conserved BC-box motif (anchored by Leu40 in a hydrophobic pocket of Elongin C), maintaining low-level transcription at PRC2 target genes [PMID:27863225, PMID:27863226, PMID:40153999]. Mechanistically, EPOP inhibits PRC2.1 by disrupting its dimerization and weakening chromatin association, thereby preventing excessive H3K27me3 deposition, while simultaneously stimulating PRC2 histone methyltransferase activity and promoting DNA-sequence-dependent (GCN-rich) chromatin binding in cooperation with MTF2 and JARID2 [PMID:41519789, PMID:41650228]. In vivo knockout of Epop causes posterior homeotic transformations of the axial skeleton due to premature Hox gene activation, establishing EPOP as a critical regulator of Polycomb-mediated developmental gene control [PMID:40834979].

ETF1 (eRF1) is the eukaryotic class-1 polypeptide chain release factor that recognizes all three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) in the ribosomal A site and catalyzes peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis to release the nascent polypeptide [PMID:7990965, PMID:10676813]. Stop codon decoding is mediated by a discontinuous recognition site in the N-terminal domain comprising the NIKS loop, the YxCxxxF motif, and residues 31–33, while the universally conserved GGQ motif in the middle domain positions a glutamine residue at the peptidyl transferase center to trigger hydrolysis; the C-terminal domain binds eRF3, whose ribosome- and eRF1-dependent GTPase activity drives conformational rearrangements essential for efficient termination, after which eRF1 marks the post-termination complex for ABCE1-mediated ribosome recycling [PMID:10445876, PMID:11911360, PMID:20688868, PMID:8634914, PMID:20122402]. eRF1 activity is modulated by GGQ glutamine N5-methylation (by the Mtq2/HemK2·Trm112 heterodimer) and NIKS lysine C4-hydroxylation (by Jmjd4), both required for optimal termination efficiency [PMID:15509572, PMID:17008308, PMID:24486019]. Beyond canonical termination, eRF1 participates in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay as a component of the SURF complex (SMG-1·Upf1·eRF1·eRF3), where competition between Upf1 and PABP for eRF3 binding at the terminating ribosome determines whether NMD is triggered [PMID:16452507, PMID:18447585].

FAM89B encodes LRAP25, a lamellipodium-localized adaptor protein that bridges MRCK kinase to LIMK1, thereby enabling MRCK-mediated phosphorylation of LIMK1 and downstream cofilin phosphorylation to control lamellipodial F-actin dynamics, cell polarization, and motility [PMID:25107909]. The FAM89B locus harbors a complex transcriptional organization encoding two open reading frames—ORF1 (the canonical LRAP25/p27 autoantigen) and ORF2—from a single gene with distinct promoters [PMID:10512749]. FAM89B protein has also been identified as an mRNA-binding protein by UV-crosslinking interactome capture in human cells, though the functional significance of this RNA-binding capacity remains uncharacterized [PMID:22658674].

GTF3C2 (TFIIIC110) is a core subunit of the human TFIIIC2 complex that recognizes B-box promoter elements and is essential for RNA polymerase III transcription of tRNA, 5S rRNA, and other non-coding RNA genes. GTF3C2 enters the nucleus, assembles with other TFIIIC subunits, and is recruited to Pol III gene loci, yet its overexpression alone is insufficient to activate Pol III transcription, indicating that TFIIIC2 complex integrity and additional regulatory inputs are required [PMID:16822860]; these inputs include physical association of the TFIIIC complex with mTOR, which couples nutrient sensing to Pol III output [PMID:20543138], interaction with NF1 to support accurate termination and reinitiation [PMID:11118217], and transcriptional control of GTF3C2 itself by Sp1 (activated upstream by GATA4 and TFAP2A) [PMID:32115405, PMID:35038452]. GTF3C2 is subject to proteolytic degradation by μ-calpain downstream of Leishmania gp63/PAR1/Ca²⁺ signaling in macrophages, which suppresses B-box-dependent ncRNA transcription and promotes pathogen survival [PMID:21149457]. Beyond canonical Pol III targets, GTF3C2 drives hepatocellular carcinoma proliferation by transcriptionally activating USP21 to stabilize MEK2 and engage ERK1/2 signaling, and it accumulates in the nucleus of cytokine-stimulated endothelial cells where it regulates claudin tight junction gene transcription [PMID:40385937, PMID:38806818].

H2AB1 (H2A.B/H2A.Bbd) is a rapidly evolving, testis-enriched histone H2A variant that generates structurally relaxed nucleosomes to facilitate transcription and RNA processing. H2A.B-containing nucleosomes wrap only ~103–118 bp of DNA in ~1.2 superhelical turns—substantially fewer than canonical nucleosomes—owing to 19 variant-specific residues including a six-residue ROF (regulating-octamer-folding) sequence and a divergent docking domain [PMID:15257289, PMID:33073403]. In human cells, H2A.B nucleosomes are enriched within actively transcribed gene bodies, and H2A.B depletion causes widespread transcriptional downregulation and aberrant mRNA splicing [PMID:22795134]. When ectopically expressed in Hodgkin lymphoma, H2A.B localizes to nucleoli, physically interacts with RNA Pol I, and drives rDNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis required for cell proliferation [PMID:34350706].

H2A.Z (encoded by H2AZ1) is a conserved histone H2A variant that is deposited into nucleosomes at promoters, enhancers, and DNA damage sites by ATP-dependent SWR1/SRCAP remodeling complexes—where the Swc2/YL1 chaperone subunit recognizes H2A.Z's C-terminal α-helix and acidic patch—and is removed by the INO80 complex and the histone chaperone ANP32E [PMID:14645854, PMID:16299513, PMID:26974124, PMID:24463511]. Once incorporated, H2A.Z stabilizes the histone octamer yet increases DNA end unwrapping and mobility, reducing the nucleosomal barrier to RNA polymerase II elongation and simultaneously enabling formation of more condensed chromatin fibers, providing a structural basis for context-dependent transcriptional activation or repression [PMID:15020582, PMID:24606920, PMID:34643712, PMID:32392318]. H2A.Z function is diversified by post-translational modifications: N-terminal acetylation by GCN5/KAT2A (selectively on the H2A.Z.1 isoform) and NuA4/Tip60 recruits BRD2 to drive transcription, monoubiquitylation by RING1b mediates Polycomb-associated gene silencing, monomethylation at K7 by SETD6 marks differentiation genes, and deSUMOylation by SENP5 promotes homologous recombination repair [PMID:31527837, PMID:17636032, PMID:23324626, PMID:37684630]. Beyond transcription, H2A.Z is loaded at DNA double-strand breaks by the p400 ATPase to facilitate BRCA1 and Ku70/Ku80 recruitment, regulates replication origin licensing through the SUV420H1–H4K20me2–ORC1 axis, and controls stem cell maintenance, neurogenesis, and memory consolidation in vivo [PMID:23122415, PMID:31875854, PMID:30842416, PMID:25219850].

IRX3 is a homeodomain transcription factor with pleiotropic roles in energy homeostasis, organ patterning, cell fate specification, and disease. Obesity-associated noncoding variants within FTO introns physically contact the IRX3 promoter via long-range chromatin interactions, establishing IRX3—not FTO—as the functional effector of the strongest common obesity-risk locus; Irx3-deficient mice are lean with increased basal metabolic rate and adipose browning, while IRX3 in hypothalamic neurons (including POMC and posterior hypothalamic populations) regulates food intake, energy expenditure, and postnatal neurogenesis of leptin-sensing arcuate neurons [PMID:24646999, PMID:33859429, PMID:40835181]. As a transcriptional regulator, IRX3 directly activates UCP1 in beige adipocytes, represses Bmp10 in endocardium to govern cardiac septation and conduction-system maturation, specifies nephron intermediate tubule identity, confers thalamic competence downstream of Shh, modulates SUMOylation-dependent epigenetic programs that maintain PPARγ activity and mesenchymal cell identity, and promotes CDK14 transcription to stabilize β-catenin in glioblastoma [PMID:28988979, PMID:22992950, PMID:17875669, PMID:24065827, PMID:40769964, PMID:41436436]. IRX3 expression is itself controlled by Wnt/β-catenin signaling through direct TCF/LEF-occupied enhancers at the IrxB locus, and aberrant activation of IRX3 via enhancer hijacking or retroviral expression drives T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and AML by immortalizing hematopoietic progenitors and blocking myeloid differentiation [PMID:32108023, PMID:39316719, PMID:29346763].

ISYNA1 encodes myo-inositol-3-phosphate synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts D-glucose-6-phosphate to 1-D-myo-inositol-3-phosphate using NAD+ as a cofactor, with activity optimally stimulated by NH4+ and K+ and strongly inhibited by Zn2+ [PMID:15024000]. ISYNA1 transcription is induced by p53 through a response element in exon 7 and is regulated by tissue-specific DNA methylation at its promoter and an intragenic differentially methylated region, while its mRNA is also modulated by glucose, statins, and the RNA-binding protein MSI2 [PMID:27035231, PMID:21841945, PMID:12941308, PMID:32779876]. ISYNA1 functions as a tumor suppressor: ectopic expression elevates intracellular myo-inositol and suppresses tumor cell growth, and epistasis experiments in pancreatic cancer cells place it in an MSI2→ISYNA1→p21/ZEB-1 axis that controls proliferation, cell cycle progression, and invasion [PMID:27035231, PMID:32779876].

KCTD2 is a BTB-domain-containing substrate adaptor for Cullin3-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes that directs ubiquitination of diverse substrates to regulate cell proliferation, GPCR signaling, and neuronal function. It recruits c-Myc for polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby suppressing glioma stem cell self-renewal and aerobic glycolysis [PMID:28060381]. KCTD2 also forms hetero-oligomers with KCTD5 to recruit Gβγ subunits in an agonist-dependent manner, promoting monoubiquitination of Gβ1/2 at K23 and attenuating Gβγ-mediated sensitization of adenylyl cyclase 5, thus shaping cAMP signaling downstream of GPCRs [PMID:34342229, PMID:36736897]. KCTD2 localizes to neuronal synapses, functionally substitutes for the Drosophila sleep regulator Insomniac in vivo, and acts redundantly with KCTD5 and KCTD17 to control cell growth and Gβ1 protein levels [PMID:28558011, PMID:38732215].

KCTD21 (also called KCASH2) functions as a BTB-domain adaptor for the Cullin3 ubiquitin ligase complex, targeting HDAC1 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation; the resulting loss of HDAC1 maintains Gli1 in an acetylated, transcriptionally inactive state, thereby suppressing Hedgehog signaling and Hedgehog-dependent cell proliferation [PMID:21472142]. KCTD21 protein stability is positively regulated by direct BTB-domain-mediated interactions with KCTD15 and KCTD1, which reduce its own ubiquitination and turnover, amplifying HDAC1 degradation and Hedgehog pathway suppression [PMID:31685809, PMID:37597490]. Transcription of KCTD21 is driven by Sp1 at a TATA-less proximal promoter in normal cells, but in p53-deficient tumor cells Sp1 instead recruits DNMT1, leading to promoter methylation and epigenetic silencing of KCTD21 expression [PMID:33898425].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: In the hair cortex, hair keratin intermediate filaments are embedded in an interfilamentous matrix, consisting of hair keratin-associated proteins (KRTAP), which are essential for the formation of a rigid and resistant hair shaft through their extensive disulfide bond cross-linking with abundant cysteine residues of hair keratins. The matrix proteins include the high-sulfur and high-glycine-tyrosine keratins (By similarity)

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: LCE1A encodes a late cornified envelope protein within the epidermal differentiation complex at chromosome 1q21 that serves as a substrate for epidermal transglutaminases and is cross-linked into the cornified envelope during terminal keratinocyte differentiation, contributing to skin barrier formation [PMID:11698679]. LCE1A is part of a coordinately regulated 'skin-expressing' LCE subgroup whose transcription is induced by calcium and ultraviolet irradiation, consistent with a role in adaptive barrier reinforcement [PMID:15854049].

MFSD12 is a major facilitator superfamily transporter that functions as the essential cysteine importer for lysosomes and melanosomes, supplying reduced cysteine (thiol) to the organellar lumen to sustain pheomelanin synthesis and lysosomal thiol homeostasis [PMID:33208952]. Loss of MFSD12 depletes melanosomal cysteine and cysteinyldopa levels and reduces lysosomal cystine accumulation in cystinosis patient fibroblasts and renal epithelial cells [PMID:33208952, PMID:38545650]. MFSD12 is essential for mouse embryonic development, with knockout embryos dying at E10.5–12.5; this lethality is rescued by the lysosome-penetrant thiol cysteamine, demonstrating that the critical function is delivery of reduced cysteine into the lysosomal lumen rather than enabling cystine export [PMID:bio_10.1101_2024.12.26.630348]. The human pigmentation-associated missense variant p.Tyr182His acts as a hypomorphic allele producing lighter coat color in knock-in mice, and MFSD12 knockdown in bladder cancer cells inhibits proliferation, migration, and metastasis downstream of transcriptional activation by PLAGL2 [PMID:37874775, PMID:41028528].

MRPL11 is a structural component of the human mitochondrial large ribosomal subunit (39S), positioned at the L7/L12 stalk where it functions alongside MRPL10 and MRPL12 to recruit translation initiation and elongation factors during mitochondrial protein synthesis [PMID:25278503, PMID:21453772]. Cryo-EM structural analysis at 3.4 Å resolution places MRPL11 within the conserved stalk architecture of the mitoribosome, which is specialized for translating mitochondrial-encoded membrane proteins required for oxidative phosphorylation [PMID:25278503]. The steady-state level of MRPL11 protein in mitochondria is regulated by the LONP1 protease; gain-of-function LONP1 mutations cause MRPL11 degradation, leading to impaired respiratory chain complex assembly [PMID:31923470]. Hybrid ribosome reconstitution experiments demonstrate functional conservation between human mitochondrial and bacterial L7/L12 stalk proteins, confirming MRPL11 as the mitochondrial ortholog of bacterial L11 [PMID:21453772].

MRPS15 is a structural component of the 28S small subunit of the mammalian mitochondrial ribosome, where it contributes to the translation of mitochondrial-encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunits [PMID:11279123, PMID:25838379]. The rate of MRPS15-dependent mitoribosomal translation modulates oxidative phosphorylation complex assembly, as demonstrated by a point mutation in the C. elegans ortholog that slows translation and suppresses mitochondrial protease deficiency [PMID:41648325]. Under endoplasmic reticulum stress, MRPS15 translocates from mitochondria to cytosolic polysomes in human cardiomyocytes, where it physically associates with cytosolic ribosomal proteins and activates IRES-dependent translation of unfolded protein response mRNAs [PMID:38542224].

MYLK2 is a calcium/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates the regulatory light chain (RLC) of myosin in skeletal muscle, thereby modulating contractile performance. Its calmodulin-binding region engages calmodulin with sub-nanomolar affinity through a classical 1-5-8-14 hydrophobic anchor motif, with distinct peptide positions contacting the N- and C-domains of calmodulin [PMID:7857920, PMID:24130683]. Genetic ablation in mice demonstrates that MYLK2-dependent RLC phosphorylation is required for post-tetanic potentiation in fast-twitch muscle [PMID:35771335], while in slow-twitch muscle, exhaustive exercise causes MYLK2 dissociation from myofilaments, leading to RLC dephosphorylation and reduced shortening capacity [PMID:25713325].

NCAPH2 (Cap-H2) is the kleisin subunit of the condensin II complex and functions as a central regulator of interphase chromatin compaction, homolog pairing, and mitotic chromosome condensation. Its chromatin loading depends on the chromo-barrel domain protein Mrg15, which binds a specific motif within NCAPH2 and is required for NCAPH2 localization to chromosomes and for condensin II-dependent chromatin reorganization [PMID:23821596, PMID:25758823]. NCAPH2 protein levels are tightly controlled by a phosphorylation–degradation axis: CK1α-dependent phosphorylation primes NCAPH2 for SCF(Slimb)-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction during interphase, while Plk1 phosphorylation at Ser288 protects NCAPH2 from Cdc20-mediated degradation and is required for its prophase accumulation and accurate chromosome condensation [PMID:23530065, PMID:25723539, PMID:28717250]. NCAPH2 also directly interacts with the shelterin component TRF1 at telomeres, where it prevents ATR-dependent DNA damage signaling and telomere fragility [PMID:31026066].

NDUFS7 (PSST) is a core catalytic subunit of mitochondrial complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) that couples electron transfer from iron-sulfur cluster N2 to ubiquinone reduction within a ~30 Å quinone-binding tunnel formed at the NDUFS7/NDUFS2(49 kDa)/ND1 interface. Conserved loop residues, including critical arginine and aspartate residues, control ubiquinone diffusion, retention, and proton translocation, while the subunit harbors the shared high-affinity binding site for structurally diverse complex I inhibitors including rotenone, piericidin A, pyridaben, and fenpyroximate [PMID:10097178, PMID:12930834, PMID:31226318, PMID:22353032]. NDUFS7 is post-translationally hydroxylated at Arg-73 by the assembly factor NDUFAF5 early in complex I biogenesis, and its loss abolishes fully assembled complex I, elevates reactive oxygen species, and triggers compensatory upregulation of the SLC7A11/glutathione axis [PMID:27226634, PMID:17604671, PMID:38823363]. NRF2 directly regulates NDUFS7 transcription, and biallelic NDUFS7 mutations cause isolated complex I deficiency [PMID:41869290, PMID:17604671].

NUP188 encodes a large scaffold nucleoporin that serves as a question-mark-shaped keystone of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) inner ring, where it establishes structural integrity, sets the resting diameter of the central transport channel, and enables NPC constriction–dilation dynamics through a linker–scaffold network with Nic96/Nup93, Nup205, Pom152, and linker nucleoporins [PMID:8682855, PMID:10831607, PMID:35679425]. Its NTR-like fold binds FG-repeat domains and allows facilitated diffusion through the NPC, blurring the classical distinction between stationary scaffold and mobile transport factors [PMID:23795296, PMID:29033133]. Beyond the NPC, NUP188 localizes to centrosomes where it directly binds Cep152 to promote centriole duplication, to mitotic spindle poles where it recruits NuMA for K-fiber formation, and to the nuclear periphery where it participates with Nup93 in HOXA gene cluster repression [PMID:32211895, PMID:23551833, PMID:27980680]. NUP188 is also required for left–right body axis patterning in Xenopus, likely via cilia-dependent signaling [PMID:21282601].

ORC2 is a core subunit of the origin recognition complex (ORC) that functions in DNA replication licensing, centromere maintenance, and replication-independent chromatin organization. ORC2 binds chromatin before S phase via its winged-helix domain in a cell-cycle-regulated manner controlled by CDK phosphorylation at Thr-116/Thr-226 (promoting dissociation) and PP1 dephosphorylation (promoting loading), with Orc1 required for initial ORC-(2–5) chromatin loading [PMID:8552193, PMID:22334659, PMID:24732362, PMID:16762929]. At centromeres, PIAS4-mediated SUMO2 modification of ORC2 recruits the demethylase KDM5A to maintain H3K4me2 levels, and loss of this SUMOylation causes heterochromatin re-replication, DNA damage, and polyploidy [PMID:27052177, PMID:29050267]. Beyond replication, DNA-bound ORC2 independently regulates chromatin compaction, repressive and activating histone marks, and CTCF-dependent chromatin loop formation at numerous genomic loci, while under replication stress Plk1 phosphorylates ORC2 at Ser188 to maintain pre-replicative complex integrity [PMID:40504688, PMID:21947279].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: Potential calcium-dependent cell-adhesion protein. May be involved in the establishment and maintenance of specific neuronal connections in the brain

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: PGK1 is a glycolytic kinase that catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoryl group from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP, generating ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate, but also functions as a regulated protein kinase with non-canonical substrates including PDHK1, Beclin1, PRAS40, and NLRP3. Its glycolytic activity is modulated by phosphorylation (T243 by PDPK1, Y324 autophosphorylation dephosphorylated by PTEN), acetylation (K220 inhibitory via KAT9/HDAC3, K323 activating via PCAF/SIRT7), crotonylation (K131/K156/K220, inhibitory), succinylation (K191/K192, stabilizing), and O-GlcNAcylation (T255, activating), while ERK-mediated S203 phosphorylation and PIN1 isomerization trigger its mitochondrial translocation where it phosphorylates PDHK1 at T338 to suppress pyruvate oxidation, and K388 acetylation by NAA10 enables its phosphorylation of Beclin1 at S30 to initiate autophagy [PMID:26942675, PMID:31911580, PMID:30029001, PMID:26356530, PMID:27774669, PMID:28486006, PMID:31492635]. PGK1 also localizes to the nucleus where CK2α-dependent S256 phosphorylation promotes its interaction with CDC7, coupling local ATP regeneration to relief of ADP-mediated inhibition of the CDC7–ASK replication initiation complex [PMID:30392930]. Beyond intracellular roles, PGK1 associates with Hsp90 to stabilize client proteins such as GSK3β and ULK1, and extracellular PGK1 engages neuronal membrane Enolase-2 to promote neurite outgrowth [PMID:34403222, PMID:37249790, PMID:37582937].

PHF8 is a JmjC-domain histone demethylase that removes mono- and di-methyl marks from H3K9, H4K20, and H3K27 in an Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent manner, functioning as a transcriptional coactivator at active gene promoters where its PHD domain reads H3K4me2/3 to direct chromatin recruitment [PMID:20622854, PMID:20622853, PMID:19843542]. Beyond histones, PHF8 demethylates non-histone substrates including TOPBP1 (K118me1) to regulate ATR kinase activation during replication stress, and YY1 to co-repress electron transport chain genes [PMID:33952527, PMID:38165927]. PHF8 protein levels and activity are dynamically controlled by phosphorylation (Cyclin E–CDK2, CK2, ERK2) and ubiquitin-mediated turnover via APC/C–CDC20, USP7, and NEDD4L, coupling its function to cell cycle progression, DNA damage repair, and signal-dependent transcriptional responses [PMID:25548279, PMID:23979597, PMID:27183383, PMID:28100697]. Loss-of-function mutations in the JmjC domain cause X-linked intellectual disability with cleft lip/palate, and Phf8 knockout mice exhibit impaired hippocampal learning/memory rescued by mTOR pathway inhibition [PMID:20622853, PMID:29317619].

PIAS4 (PIASy) is a SUMO E3 ligase that conjugates SUMO-1, SUMO-2, and SUMO-3 to a broad spectrum of substrates to regulate transcription, DNA damage repair, mitotic chromosome segregation, innate immunity, and metabolic signaling. Its E3 ligase activity requires two C-terminal SUMO-interacting motifs (SIMs) and typically its RING-finger-like (SP-RING) domain, although certain substrates such as YY1 are SUMOylated in a RING-independent manner; PIAS4 also represses transcription through SUMO-independent mechanisms involving HDAC1/HDAC2 recruitment via its RD1 domain and nuclear-matrix sequestration of substrates via its SAP domain [PMID:11731474, PMID:14981544, PMID:18477566, PMID:17353273, PMID:28455449]. At DNA double-strand breaks, PIAS4 accumulates via its SAP domain and drives SUMO accrual that is essential for 53BP1, BRCA1, and RNF168 recruitment, ubiquitin-adduct formation, and homologous recombination; on mitotic chromosomes, its N-terminal domain binds the Rod/Zw10 kinetochore complex to direct centromeric SUMOylation of Topoisomerase IIα and PARP1, controlling decatenation and sister chromatid segregation [PMID:20016603, PMID:35007836, PMID:15933717, PMID:20696768, PMID:21079245]. PIAS4 protein stability is regulated by TRIM32- and FIEL1 (KIAA0317)-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, linking its abundance to stress signaling and TGF-β pathway output [PMID:16816390, PMID:27162139].

POU5F1 (OCT4) is a POU-domain transcription factor that functions as a quantitative master regulator of pluripotency, where precise expression levels dictate whether embryonic stem cells self-renew, differentiate into trophectoderm, or adopt primitive endoderm/mesoderm fates [PMID:10742100, PMID:9814708]. It heterodimerizes with SOX2 on composite sox-oct cis-regulatory elements to drive autoregulatory and feedforward transcriptional circuits—including activation of NANOG, FGF4, and LIN28B—and cooperates with KLF4 to activate additional ES-specific targets [PMID:16153702, PMID:15860457, PMID:19816951]. Structurally, OCT4 employs a unique surface-exposed α-helical linker between its POU sub-domains as a protein–protein interaction hub that recruits competing co-regulators (Klf5, Cbx1, Set1a, β-catenin, Dax1), and uses both POUS and POUHD domains to engage and cooperatively unwrap nucleosomal DNA as a pioneer transcription factor [PMID:23376973, PMID:35171666, PMID:32327602, PMID:37327775]. Its activity is modulated by ERK2-mediated phosphorylation at T234/S235 (which disrupts DNA binding), SirT1-dependent deacetylation (which gates the naive-to-primed transition), and sumoylation (required for G1/S progression), integrating signaling inputs to control cell-cycle progression and lineage commitment [PMID:22474382, PMID:27732856, PMID:23495099].

PRH1 encodes the acidic proline-rich salivary protein Pa (and its allelic variants Db and PIF), a secreted protein enriched in proline, glutamic acid, and glycine, with a low isoelectric point and minimal carbohydrate content [PMID:803013]. A cysteine substitution near Arg106 unique to the Pa allele sterically prevents proteolytic cleavage at that site, producing a single-banded electrophoretic phenotype, whereas the Db and PIF alleles are cleaved at Arg106 to yield double-banded products; the Db allele additionally carries a 21-amino acid repeat insertion accounting for its larger size [PMID:3687941]. The Pa protein forms disulfide-bonded complexes with salivary peroxidase (SAPX1) to generate the SAPX2 complex in human parotid saliva [PMID:849256].

PSMB3 encodes the beta-3 subunit of the 20S proteasome core particle, which assembles with other alpha and beta subunits to form the multicatalytic threonine protease complex that, together with the 19S regulatory particle, constitutes the 26S proteasome responsible for ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation [PMID:8811196, PMID:10436176]. Beyond its general housekeeping role in proteostasis, PSMB3-dependent proteasome activity is specifically required for FANCD2 monoubiquitination in the Fanconi anemia DNA damage response [PMID:17671210], for CTG·CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in human cells [PMID:23620289], and for restricting adeno-associated virus trafficking through the secretory pathway [PMID:21625534]. Basal PSMB3 transcription in cancer cells is maintained by an NFE2L1/NFE2L3–CPEB3 regulatory axis, and its depletion impairs overall proteasome capacity, sensitizing myeloma cells to bortezomib and triggering compensatory transcriptional responses such as TRIB1 induction in hepatocytes [PMID:32366381, PMID:21289309, PMID:37291259]. The human PSMB3 locus maps to chromosome 2q35, independently of the MHC-linked inducible proteasome subunit genes [PMID:9344661].

PSMD13 is a non-ATPase subunit of the 19S regulatory particle lid of the 26S proteasome, essential for efficient proteasome assembly and ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation. Its C-terminal PCI domain mediates interaction with the neighboring lid subunit Rpn5, while its N-terminal domain recruits the ubiquitin receptor Rpn10 into the 26S proteasome, as revealed by high-resolution NMR structure determination of the yeast ortholog Rpn9 [PMID:25631053, PMID:10490597]. Loss of PSMD13/Rpn9 causes temperature-sensitive growth, accumulation of multiubiquitinated proteins, and defective proteasome assembly [PMID:10490597, PMID:9714768]. Beyond its core proteasomal role, PSMD13 suppresses NF-κB signaling by inhibiting K63-linked ubiquitination of TAK1 [PMID:37257570], supports hematopoietic stem cell repopulating capacity and megakaryocytic differentiation downstream of IL-4 [PMID:37653079], and associates with Dicer to modulate miR-29a levels during neuronal differentiation [PMID:41734180].

PTGES3 (p23) is a co-chaperone of Hsp90 that stabilizes the ATP-bound closed conformation of the Hsp90 dimer, thereby facilitating the maturation, folding, and stabilization of diverse client proteins including steroid hormone receptors (GR, PR, ER, AR), telomerase (hTERT), the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR), and chromatin remodeling complexes such as RSC [PMID:7929183, PMID:16625188, PMID:34937936, PMID:27818141]. p23 binds Hsp90 via its N-terminal beta-sandwich domain at the interface of the Hsp90 N-terminal and middle domains in a 2:2 stoichiometry, while its unstructured C-terminal tail mediates Hsp90-independent chaperoning of non-native substrates, direct client contacts (e.g., stabilizing native GR via a C-terminal helix), and protection of clients such as AHR from ubiquitin-mediated degradation [PMID:10543959, PMID:34937936, PMID:29555469, PMID:21183720]. p23 additionally promotes receptor–DNA dissociation to dynamically regulate transcription factor occupancy at target genes and modulates telomerase DNA binding and extension in a cell-cycle-dependent manner [PMID:10691735, PMID:17389357]. During apoptosis, caspase-3/7 cleavage of p23 at D142/D145 generates a dominant-negative fragment that disrupts Hsp90 function, destabilizes clients including hTERT, and sensitizes cells to death; p23-null mice die perinatally with glucocorticoid receptor-deficient phenotypes, confirming its essential in vivo role in GR signaling rather than prostaglandin E2 biosynthesis [PMID:15483679, PMID:19740745, PMID:17000766, PMID:17438133].

RAB10 is a small GTPase that serves as a master regulator of membrane trafficking across diverse cellular contexts, directing vesicle translocation, endocytic recycling, organelle dynamics, and autophagy. In adipocytes, RAB10 acts downstream of the AS160/TBC1D4 GAP and is activated by the GEF Dennd4C to drive insulin-stimulated GLUT4 storage vesicle translocation to the plasma membrane, engaging effectors including Myosin-Va, the exocyst subunits Exoc6/Exoc6b, SEC16A, and the Ral-GEF Rlf/RalA cascade [PMID:17403373, PMID:21454697, PMID:22908308, PMID:26299925, PMID:25103239]; in epithelial cells and neurons, RAB10 controls basolateral endocytic recycling (with EHBP-1), tubular endosome formation (via KIF13A/KIF13B), ER tubule dynamics, phagosome maturation, lipophagy (with EHBP1 and EHD2), TLR4 surface delivery, and anterograde axonal transport through a kinesin-1/JIP1 complex released by Lgl1-mediated GDI displacement [PMID:16394106, PMID:30700496, PMID:23263280, PMID:20028485, PMID:28028537, PMID:20643919, PMID:24478353, PMID:21856246]. RAB10 is a principal substrate of the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2, which phosphorylates Thr73 in the switch-II motif; pathogenic LRRK2 mutations hyperphosphorylate RAB10, impairing its interaction with OPTN to block mitophagy and redirecting phospho-RAB10 to RILPL1/RILPL2 at mother centriole subdistal appendages to disrupt ciliogenesis and centrosomal cohesion [PMID:27474410, PMID:30945962, PMID:33653948, PMID:35776681]. LRRK2-mediated RAB10 phosphorylation on lysosomes is spatially regulated by perinuclear lysosome positioning and opposed by the phosphatase PPM1H, and phospho-RAB10 interacts with VPS13C to mediate lysosomal stress responses in dopaminergic neurons [PMID:36256825, PMID:38358348].

RAD54L2 (ARIP4) is a SNF2-family ATPase that couples SUMO-dependent protein recognition with chromatin remodeling to maintain genome stability and regulate transcription. Its ATPase activity is stimulated by sumoylated nuclear receptors on DNA and is required for resolving TOP2 cleavage complexes—acting with ZATT/ZNF451 and TDP2 to promote TOP2 turnover from chromatin and prevent accumulation of TOP2-DNA crosslinks and double-strand breaks [PMID:38055811, PMID:38055822, PMID:19692572]. RAD54L2 also directly binds and unwinds R-loops at transcription start sites to facilitate release of paused RNA Pol II during androgen-dependent transcription, and interacts with BLM helicase to recruit it to chromatin and suppress sister chromatid exchanges, thereby favoring non-crossover recombination outcomes [PMID:39028815, PMID:39870965]. Its protein stability is regulated by p62/SQSTM1-mediated selective autophagy [PMID:26412716].

RAN is a small GTPase whose asymmetric nucleotide cycle—GTP loading by chromatin-bound RCC1 in the nucleus and GTP hydrolysis stimulated by cytoplasmic RanGAP1—creates a steep RanGTP/RanGDP gradient across the nuclear envelope that powers nucleocytoplasmic transport of proteins and RNAs by controlling the assembly and disassembly of importin/exportin–cargo complexes [PMID:8146159, PMID:7937864, PMID:8896452, PMID:9323133]. During mitosis, chromosome-generated RanGTP liberates spindle assembly factors (TPX2, Aurora A, HURP, hKid) from importin inhibition, driving microtubule nucleation, kinetochore-fiber organization, and spindle pole formation, with CRM1 recruiting RanGAP1/RanBP2 to kinetochores for local gradient shaping [PMID:12577065, PMID:15908946, PMID:16631581, PMID:18268099]. RAN activity is tuned by post-translational modifications—PAK4-mediated Ser-135 phosphorylation modulates RCC1/RanGAP1 interactions, CBP/p300- and TIP60-mediated lysine acetylation regulates nucleotide exchange and Mog1 displacement, and RanBP2-complex-mediated SUMOylation targets RanGDP at the NPC—while RanGTP also functions outside the nucleus at centrosomes (via AKAP450), basal bodies during ciliogenesis, and the plasma membrane where it stabilizes RhoA to promote cell invasion [PMID:20805321, PMID:26124124, PMID:29040603, PMID:26251516, PMID:14517334, PMID:21998203, PMID:31209254].

RBM17 (SPF45) is a spliceosomal RNA-binding protein that regulates both constitutive and alternative pre-mRNA splicing, with additional roles in DNA repair and cell-cycle control. Its UHM domain competes with U2AF65 for binding to SF3b155 ULM motifs, enabling spliceosome assembly on short introns with truncated polypyrimidine tracts, and it activates the 3′ splice site for the second catalytic step of splicing [PMID:12015979, PMID:17589525, PMID:34389706]. RBM17 forms a ternary complex with U2SURP and CHERP that co-regulates alternative splicing of cell-cycle genes including FOXM1, controls G2/M progression, and represses cryptic splicing events essential for neuronal survival, as demonstrated by embryonic lethality and Purkinje cell degeneration in Rbm17-knockout mice [PMID:30332651, PMID:34544891, PMID:28007900]. Its splicing activity is modulated by phosphorylation from ERK2, JNK1, p38, Clk1, and AKT1, and in leukemic stem cells RBM17 suppresses poison-exon inclusion in transcripts such as EIF4A2 to sustain pro-leukemic gene expression programs [PMID:22615491, PMID:23519612, PMID:36520054, PMID:35781533].

RPL13 (eL13) is an integral protein of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that functions in canonical mRNA translation and possesses extraribosomal regulatory activities. Structurally resolved at near-atomic resolution within the human 80S ribosome [PMID:25901680], RPL13 is required for proper 60S–80S subunit dynamics and global translation, as patient-derived missense variants alter the 60S:80S ratio and attenuate protein synthesis [PMID:32916022]. Beyond its core ribosomal role, RPL13 selectively promotes viral IRES-driven translation by cooperating with DDX3 and eIF3 subunits to facilitate 80S assembly on viral mRNAs [PMID:31619563], and it modulates NF-κB/IFN-β innate immune signaling [PMID:34093518]. Pathogenic variants in RPL13 — clustering in an RNA-binding motif — cause spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with severe short stature, establishing it as a ribosomopathy gene essential for skeletal and cardiac development [PMID:31630789, PMID:31625562].

RPL14 (eL14) is an essential structural component of the 60S large ribosomal subunit that assembles into pre-60S particles at an early nucleolar stage, where it is required for processing of 27SA2/27SA3 pre-rRNAs to 27SB and for subsequent nuclear export of pre-60S intermediates [PMID:29788267]. Structurally, RPL14 adopts a five-stranded beta-barrel fold with two rRNA-binding surfaces and a hydrophobic protein-interaction patch that mediates contact with neighboring protein L19, and its eukaryote-specific C-terminal extension functionally cooperates with that of L16 to influence translation [PMID:8805509, PMID:29788267]. Haploinsufficiency of RPL14 produces the classic Minute phenotype in Drosophila, while complete depletion is lethal, underscoring its essential role in ribosome biogenesis and cell viability [PMID:9236770, PMID:14597387]. PRMT5-mediated symmetric dimethylation of RPL14 at arginine residues stabilizes the protein and promotes DNA damage repair, linking ribosomal protein modification to genotoxic stress responses in cancer cells [PMID:40115921].

RPL24 (eL24) is a large ribosomal subunit protein that functions as an assembly-initiator protein, binding the 5′ domain I of 23S/28S rRNA (positions ~99–107) to nucleate early rRNA folding and 50S/60S subunit biogenesis [PMID:357435, PMID:404143, PMID:3278299]. In eukaryotes, eL24 forms two intersubunit bridges (eB13 and B6) required for 60S–40S subunit joining and translation initiation, and its haploinsufficiency activates a p53–p21 checkpoint and suppresses tumorigenesis by promoting eEF2K-dependent phosphorylation of eEF2 to reduce translation elongation rates [PMID:30407570, PMID:19273598, PMID:34895463]. RPL24 depletion selectively reduces cap-dependent (eIF4E-dependent) translation of oncogenic mRNAs such as cyclin D1 and survivin [PMID:24970821]. An extra-ribosomal function has been identified in which RPL24 interacts with DDX5 to inhibit Microprocessor-mediated miRNA biogenesis [PMID:38261097].

RPL39L is a testis-enriched autosomal retrogene of the X-linked ribosomal protein RPL39 that assembles into a specialized ribosome (RibosomeST) with a structurally distinct nascent polypeptide exit tunnel, thereby promoting cotranslational folding of alpha-helical domains in a subset of male germ-cell-specific proteins essential for spermatogenesis [PMID:36517592, PMID:39041433]. RPL39L arose by retrotransposition and is expressed predominantly in testis, likely compensating for X-chromosome inactivation during male meiosis [PMID:12490704]. Deletion of Rpl39l in mice causes reduced spermatogonial stem cell proliferation, malformed sperm mitochondria and flagella, impaired protein synthesis and ribosome subunit biogenesis, and widespread autophagy—defects that cannot be rescued by the canonical RPL39-containing ribosome [PMID:34825148, PMID:36517592, PMID:39041433]. RPL39L also supports pluripotency and differentiation in embryonic stem cells, and combined loss of both RPL39 and RPL39L activates protein misfolding pathways and inhibits preimplantation embryo development [PMID:39041433, PMID:40421595].

SIGLEC6 encodes an inhibitory I-type lectin of the Siglec family that transduces sialic acid-dependent extracellular signals into intracellular phosphatase cascades, functioning as a broad-spectrum negative regulator of cell activation in mast cells and trophoblasts while paradoxically promoting migration in CLL and AML cells. Siglec-6 selectively recognizes Neu5Acα2-6GalNAcα (sialyl-Tn) and membrane-embedded gangliosides — the latter through canonical Arg122-mediated sialic acid coordination supplemented by phospholipid membrane contacts via Lys126 and Trp127 — and also binds leptin with high affinity [PMID:10428856, PMID:41606261]. Its cytoplasmic ITIM and ITIM-like motifs are phosphorylated by Src family kinases, enabling recruitment of SHP-1 and SHP-2: in mast cells this suppresses FcεRI-, KIT/SCF-, and MRGPRX2-mediated degranulation by dampening ERK1/2 and p38 signaling, while in trophoblasts it inhibits NF-κB and ERK/c-Jun pathways to restrain invasion, and its overexpression induces a preeclampsia-like phenotype in mice [PMID:36359823, PMID:38186079, PMID:39039496, PMID:21880722]. In CLL B cells, Siglec-6 engages the DOCK8–Cdc42–WASP axis to drive F-actin polymerization and cell migration, and in AML cells it activates SHP-2/Src/ERK signaling to promote proliferation and invasion [PMID:38890323, PMID:40436895].

SKP1 is a core adaptor subunit of SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein) E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes that bridges F-box proteins to the CUL1 scaffold, thereby enabling ubiquitin-dependent degradation of phosphorylated substrates including IκBα, β-catenin, cyclin E, p21, cyclin D, securin, and PFKFB3 [PMID:11961546, PMID:10230406, PMID:10023660, PMID:9736735, PMID:17434132]. SKP1 engages F-box proteins through a bipartite interface involving both the F-box motif and adjacent substrate-recognition domains, and productive SCF assembly is regulated by CUL1 neddylation—which displaces the inhibitor CAND1—and by substrate engagement that protects the complex from CSN-mediated deneddylation [PMID:11099048, PMID:12504025, PMID:22767593]. Beyond its ubiquitin ligase role, SKP1 functions at kinetochores as a subunit of the budding yeast CBF3 centromere-binding complex, interacts with Bub1 to transduce spindle checkpoint signals in response to loss of kinetochore tension, and associates with CENP-E at the midbody to regulate cytokinesis; loss of SKP1 function causes chromosome missegregation, replication stress, and genomic instability [PMID:8706132, PMID:12769845, PMID:16682006, PMID:12417738, PMID:32106628]. In Dictyostelium, O₂-dependent prolyl hydroxylation and subsequent cytoplasmic pentasaccharide glycosylation of Skp1 Pro143 remodel the F-box-combining domain to promote F-box protein binding, representing a unique post-translational regulatory mechanism [PMID:9660787, PMID:28928219, PMID:25341530].

SLC39A7 (ZIP7) is an ER-resident zinc transporter that gates the release of Zn²⁺ from ER/Golgi stores into the cytosol, functioning as a central node linking intracellular zinc homeostasis to cell signaling, ER proteostasis, and cell fate decisions. CK2-mediated phosphorylation at conserved serine residues (S275, S276, and two additional sites) activates ZIP7, triggering a cytosolic zinc wave that inhibits phosphatases and thereby potentiates tyrosine kinase, MAPK, PI3K-AKT, and mTOR signaling [PMID:22317921, PMID:28205653, PMID:18583420]. Loss of ZIP7 causes ER zinc accumulation, protein disulfide isomerase aggregation, ER stress, impaired ERAD—partly through reduced Zn²⁺ supply to the Rpn11 proteasomal deubiquitinase—and defective secretory pathway trafficking of Notch and death receptors [PMID:28545780, PMID:38670102, PMID:23785054, PMID:30237509]. Hypomorphic SLC39A7 mutations in humans cause a block in early B cell development due to insufficient cytosolic zinc and excessive phosphatase activity that attenuates pre-BCR/BCR signaling [PMID:30918914].

SLC41A1 is the principal mammalian Na⁺/Mg²⁺ exchanger responsible for cellular Mg²⁺ efflux, with broad downstream consequences for Ca²⁺ signaling, pro-survival kinase pathways, osteogenesis, synaptic transmission, and inflammasome-driven pyroptosis. SLC41A1 localizes to the plasma membrane (basolateral in polarized epithelia), adopts a 10-transmembrane-helix topology with cytoplasmic termini, and mediates Na⁺-dependent Mg²⁺ extrusion that is inhibited by imipramine and quinidine and regulated by cAMP/PKA, insulin/PI3K, and p38 MAPK signaling [PMID:22031603, PMID:26355001, PMID:30417250]. Surface abundance of SLC41A1 is itself controlled by Mg²⁺-dependent endosomal recycling through its N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, and STAT5A-driven transcriptional upregulation couples SLC41A1 to mitochondrial permeability transition and AIM2 inflammasome activation [PMID:21696366, PMID:40831212]. A homozygous splice-site mutation in SLC41A1 that deletes a transmembrane helix abolishes Mg²⁺ transport and is associated with nephronophthisis-like renal disease, while the Parkinson-disease-linked p.A350V variant is a gain-of-function allele that enhances Mg²⁺ efflux and disrupts cAMP-dependent regulation [PMID:23661805, PMID:23976986].

SNAPC4 (SNAP190) is the largest subunit of the five-subunit SNAPc complex and serves as the central scaffold for snRNA gene transcription by both RNA polymerase II and III. Its 4.5-repeat Myb DNA-binding domain directly recognizes the proximal sequence element (PSE) of snRNA promoters in a wrap-around mode together with SNAP50 and SNAP43, while also recruiting TBP to the adjacent TATA box and providing the docking surface for cooperative activation by the Oct-1 POU domain [PMID:9418884, PMID:36369505, PMID:12414730, PMID:12391172]. CK2 phosphorylation of the SNAP190 N-terminal region allosterically inhibits its DNA-binding activity, and proper complex assembly depends on SUMOylation of the SNAPC1 subunit to maintain the SNAPC1–SNAPC4 interaction [PMID:17670747, PMID:40956881]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function SNAPC4 variants in humans cause reduced snRNA levels, global alternative splicing dysregulation, and a neurodegenerative disorder featuring neuroregression and progressive spastic paraparesis [PMID:36965478].

TAF1B is a TFIIB-related subunit of the RNA polymerase I selectivity factor SL1 that functions as a core component of the Pol I pre-initiation complex at ribosomal DNA promoters, playing an essential role in rRNA gene transcription. TAF1B assembles with TBP and the other TAF_I subunits (TAF1A, TAF1C, TAF1D) to form the SL1 complex, which binds the rDNA promoter both independently and cooperatively with UBF, stabilizing UBF occupancy and recruiting initiation-competent Pol I via interaction with hRRN3 [PMID:1547496, PMID:7801130, PMID:15970593, PMID:11250903]. Structurally homologous to TFIIB through N-terminal zinc ribbon and cyclin-like fold domains, TAF1B fulfills an essential post-polymerase recruitment function analogous to TFIIB in Pol II transcription [PMID:21921199]. TAF1B activity is regulated by PCAF-mediated acetylation, which enhances rDNA promoter binding and stimulates transcription, by mSir2a-mediated deacetylation, which represses transcription, and by cdc2/cyclin B phosphorylation of SL1 during mitosis, which inactivates the complex [PMID:11250901, PMID:9857193].

TBATA (also known as SPATIAL) is expressed in thymic stromal cells and functions as a negative regulator of thymic epithelial cell (TEC) proliferation by binding the neddylation enzyme Uba3 and inhibiting the Nedd8 conjugation pathway [PMID:20937703]. Loss of Tbata in aged mice leads to thymic enlargement with increased TEC proliferation and accelerated thymic reconstitution after bone marrow transplantation, establishing TBATA as a cell-intrinsic brake on thymus size and regenerative capacity [PMID:20937703].

TFPT (also called Amida/FB1) is a nuclear protein that binds DNA through a central domain (aa 76–189) flanked by two nuclear localization signals, and its overexpression induces S-phase arrest and caspase 9-dependent, p53-independent apoptosis in a cell-type- and proliferation-dependent manner [PMID:12841360, PMID:17041757]. TFPT interacts with Cdc2 during mitosis, and Cdc2-mediated phosphorylation at Ser-180 negatively regulates TFPT's DNA-binding activity, linking cell cycle progression to TFPT function [PMID:12841360]. Par-4 recruits TFPT from the nucleus to cytoplasmic actin filaments, synergistically enhancing apoptosis through myosin II regulatory light chain phosphorylation [PMID:16229834], while TFPT also inhibits the transcriptional activity of the tumor suppressor EAF2 and co-localizes with the elongation factor ELL in the nucleus [PMID:17395368]. TFPT expression is driven by a TATA-less promoter responsive to the hematopoietic transcription factors PU.1 and Ikaros 2, arranged head-to-head with the PRPF31 promoter with partially overlapping but distinct regulatory elements [PMID:11700047, PMID:22723017].

THOC5 is a subunit of the THO/TREX complex that functions as a selective mRNA export adaptor, coupling transcription elongation, 3'-end processing, and nuclear export for a specific subset of mRNAs critical to hematopoietic stem cell maintenance, lineage commitment, and stress-responsive gene expression. THOC5 binds the NTF2-like domain of the export receptor NXF1/Tap at a site distinct from Aly, enabling simultaneous adaptor engagement, and directly associates with 3'-end processing factors CFIm68 and CPSF100 to control polyadenylation site choice — its depletion causes widespread alternative cleavage and failure to release select transcripts from chromatin [PMID:19165146, PMID:23685434, PMID:25274738]. THOC5 also modulates transcription elongation rate, forming a chromatin-associated complex with CDK12, DDX5, and DDX17 that promotes CDK12 recruitment to R-loops in a THOC6-dependent manner [PMID:36590164]. Multiple signaling kinases regulate THOC5 function: PKC phosphorylation at S5/S6 controls its nuclear–cytoplasmic shuttling, ATM phosphorylation at S307/S312/S314 suppresses its mRNA-binding capacity upon DNA damage, and Src-mediated Y225 phosphorylation modulates RNA binding in hematopoietic cells [PMID:15221008, PMID:21937706, PMID:23032722].

TMEM63A is a mechanosensitive nonselective cation channel with a monomeric eleven-transmembrane-helix architecture that is gated by membrane tension to produce sustained, voltage-independent, Gd³⁺-sensitive cation currents without inactivation [PMID:38217391, PMID:38189136]. Ca²⁺ influx through TMEM63A drives oligodendrocyte precursor cell differentiation and myelination—heterozygous pore-domain missense variants cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 19 (HLD19) by attenuating stretch-activated currents and blocking channel trafficking to the plasma membrane [PMID:31587869, PMID:39982638, PMID:40694323]. On lysosomal membranes, TMEM63A relieves hydrostatic pressure by conducting monovalent cations out of the lumen, protecting lysosomes from tension-induced lysis, and it interacts with VCP and DERL1 to regulate autophagic protein turnover [PMID:41811130, PMID:35920704]. In alveolar type 2 cells, TMEM63A localizes to lamellar body membranes where its activation during cell stretch facilitates pulmonary surfactant and ATP release, coupling mechanotransduction to exocytic Ca²⁺ signaling [PMID:38127458].

TOP2A is a type IIA DNA topoisomerase that resolves topological constraints—catenanes, knots, and supercoils—by introducing transient double-strand breaks through a 5′-phosphotyrosyl covalent intermediate, functioning in DNA replication, transcription, chromatin remodeling, and chromosome segregation [PMID:1331984, PMID:8395511, PMID:20797631]. Genome-wide mapping reveals two classes of TOP2A cleavage: CTCF-proximal sites and transcription-associated cleavage enriched at gene bodies, where TOP2A synergizes with BAF chromatin remodelers to convert facultative heterochromatin to accessible chromatin via decatenation [PMID:31649282, PMID:28385713, PMID:28250416]. TOP2A is recruited to ultra-fine anaphase bridges by TOPBP1 and directed toward decatenation by condensin relocalization during anaphase; at stalled replication forks, ZATT-mediated SUMOylation of TOP2A recruits the translocase PICH to drive fork reversal [PMID:25762097, PMID:27716481, PMID:26686624, PMID:33296677]. Trapped TOP2A–DNA cleavage complexes are resolved by complementary repair pathways including Tdp1- and TDP2-mediated phosphotyrosyl hydrolysis, ubiquitin- and VCP/p97-dependent proteasomal degradation, and SUMO-targeted translocase protection, while TOP2A protein stability is regulated by Bmi1/Ring1A ubiquitination and PTEN/OTUD3 deubiquitination [PMID:16751265, PMID:26421495, PMID:32587095, PMID:33941661, PMID:28552615, PMID:19956605, PMID:26657567].

TRNP1 is a low-complexity, intrinsically disordered nuclear protein that functions as a dose-dependent regulator of neural stem cell fate during cerebral cortex development: high TRNP1 levels promote NSC self-renewal and tangential cortical expansion, whereas reduced levels drive production of intermediate progenitors and basal radial glia, enabling radial expansion and cortical folding [PMID:23622239]. TRNP1 undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation via its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region and co-regulates the architecture of multiple nuclear membrane-less compartments—nucleolus, nuclear speckles, and condensed chromatin—linking nuclear condensate organization to cell-cycle control in neural progenitors [PMID:32627867]. TMF/ARA160 binds TRNP1 and directs it to proteasomal degradation, providing a post-translational mechanism for tuning TRNP1 protein levels [PMID:16792503]. The rate of TRNP1 coding-sequence evolution across mammals correlates with brain size and cortical folding, and species-specific TRNP1 variants differ in their ability to drive NSC proliferation [PMID:36947129].

TXN (thioredoxin-1) is a ubiquitous cytosolic dithiol oxidoreductase with a CGPC active site that serves as the principal protein disulfide reductase and electron donor for ribonucleotide reductases, peroxiredoxins, and methionine sulfoxide reductases, while also functioning as a secreted cytokine and a central node in redox-dependent signaling [PMID:11012661, PMID:2785919]. In its reduced state, TXN directly binds and inhibits ASK1 kinase; oxidation or TXNIP binding disrupts this complex, unleashing ASK1-dependent JNK/p38 apoptotic signaling [PMID:9564042, PMID:10419473]. TXN translocates to the nucleus upon oxidative or nitrosative stress—regulated by ERK1/2-mediated downregulation of TXNIP—where it reduces Ref-1 to potentiate AP-1 and HIF-1α transcriptional activity, and it acts as a protein denitrosylase (with thioredoxin reductase) that removes S-nitrosylation from caspase-3 to control apoptosis [PMID:9108029, PMID:18497292, PMID:24376827]. A proteolytic fragment (Trx80) functions as a redox-independent cytokine that activates monocytes and induces IL-12 secretion [PMID:11342447].

UBE2Q1 is an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme that functions as a pro-proliferative and anti-apoptotic factor by promoting ubiquitin-dependent degradation of p53 and stabilizing β-catenin to activate downstream oncogenic signaling cascades. UBE2Q1 physically interacts with and downregulates p53 protein levels in breast cancer and neuronal cells, and its knockdown increases p53 abundance and sensitizes cells to apoptosis [PMID:25987028, PMID:24166684]. In colorectal and hepatocellular carcinoma cells, UBE2Q1 stabilizes β-catenin to drive EGFR–PI3K–Akt–mTOR signaling, HIF-1α–dependent glycolysis, cell cycle progression into S phase, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition [PMID:29027712, PMID:35156520, PMID:27602158]. Ube2q1-knockout female mice exhibit impaired oestrus cycling, reduced embryo implantation, and increased embryonic lethality, establishing a requirement for this enzyme in mammalian female fertility [PMID:23108111].

VPS25 is a core subunit of the ESCRT-II complex that bridges ESCRT-I to ESCRT-III during multivesicular body biogenesis, functioning through two tandem winged-helix domains, the second of which directly engages the ESCRT-III subunit VPS20/CHMP6 to activate membrane budding and scission required for lysosomal degradation of ubiquitinated cargo such as EGFR and FGFR [PMID:15579210, PMID:19686684, PMID:15511219, PMID:16973552]. In Drosophila, VPS25 acts as a tumor suppressor: its loss causes endosomal accumulation of Notch and Dpp receptors, ectopic activation of Notch, JAK-STAT, and Hippo signaling, and non-autonomous overgrowth that can progress to metastasis when apoptosis is blocked [PMID:16256743, PMID:16256745, PMID:16611691]. VPS25 selectively modulates receptor tyrosine kinase trafficking in vertebrate development, as a hypomorphic mouse allele perturbs FGFR degradation and causes polydactyly without affecting SHH or WNT signaling [PMID:25373905]. Beyond its canonical ESCRT role, VPS25 directly binds RNA through recognition of a polypurine (GA-rich) motif, revealing an additional molecular activity for ESCRT-II [PMID:29903915].

VPS28 is a core subunit of the ESCRT-I complex that functions as a central adaptor linking ubiquitinated cargo recognition to downstream membrane remodeling during multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis, viral budding, phagophore closure, and cytokinesis. Its N-terminal region binds directly to TSG101/VPS23 to assemble ESCRT-I, while its independently folded C-terminal four-helical-bundle domain recruits ESCRT-III via direct interaction with Vps20, a connection essential for membrane scission events including retroviral budding [PMID:16749904, PMID:11134028]. VPS28-dependent endosomal sorting is required for degradation of ubiquitinated receptors such as EGFR [PMID:11916981], for neuronal extracellular vesicle secretion that supports brain angiogenesis [PMID:35330682], and for phagophore closure during autophagy [PMID:36907049]. Loss of VPS28 also causes lysosome-dependent transcriptional reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis via NF-κB and JNK pathway activation [PMID:12663786, PMID:8817003].

VPS41 is a conserved subunit of the HOPS tethering complex that controls membrane fusion at the late endosome–lysosome interface and, independently of HOPS, functions as a coat-like scaffold in regulated secretory granule biogenesis. Within HOPS, VPS41 is recruited via a metazoan-specific RING–RING interaction with VPS18 [PMID:28931724] and employs an ALPS motif whose phosphorylation by Yck3 (yeast) or p38α-MAPK (mammals) acts as a curvature-sensing switch that directs the complex between endosome–vacuole and AP-3 vesicle–vacuole fusion routes [PMID:21079247, PMID:23245320]; VPS41 also recruits TGN-derived LAMP carriers through its WD40 domain interaction with the GTPase Arl8b, thereby delivering NPC1 and other lysosomal membrane proteins and maintaining cholesterol homeostasis [PMID:39907656, PMID:41452985]. In a HOPS-independent capacity, VPS41 self-assembles into a lattice that cooperates with AP-3 to sort dense-core vesicle and insulin secretory granule cargo, and β-cell-specific VPS41 deletion causes diabetes in mice [PMID:24210660, PMID:33168621]; biallelic loss-of-function VPS41 variants in humans cause infantile-onset dystonia and progressive cerebellar ataxia with impaired lysosomal function [PMID:32808683, PMID:33764426].

VTI1B is a Qb-SNARE protein that functions as a versatile fusogenic component in endosomal, lysosomal, and autophagic membrane trafficking by assembling into distinct four-helix SNARE complexes with partners including syntaxin 6, syntaxin 7, syntaxin 8, syntaxin 11, VAMP8, VAMP3, and VAMP4. VTI1B is required for late endosome–lysosome fusion, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, recycling endosome–autophagosome fusion during xenophagy, and Golgi-to-late-endosome transport of cargo such as TNFα and MT1-MMP; its loss leads to accumulation of multivesicular bodies and autophagic vacuoles, degradation of its stabilizing partner syntaxin 8, and impaired lysosomal degradation [PMID:12861006, PMID:20089838, PMID:27791468, PMID:34476885]. PTPN9-mediated dephosphorylation of VTI1B promotes SNARE complex assembly and autophagic flux, while selective incorporation of VTI1B into clathrin-coated vesicles requires the adaptor epsinR [PMID:33112705, PMID:15371541]. VTI1B has specialized roles in lytic granule exocytosis in cytotoxic T lymphocytes, TNFα secretion in macrophages, and modulation of TRPV1-dependent inflammatory pain sensitization in sensory neurons, and combined loss of Vti1a and Vti1b causes perinatal lethality with massive peripheral neurodegeneration [PMID:20543108, PMID:15640147, PMID:30335684, PMID:21262811].

WBP11 (also known as SIPP1/NpwBP) is a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling pre-mRNA splicing factor that localizes to nuclear speckles and spliceosomes, where it activates splicing in a concentration-dependent manner and inhibits protein phosphatase-1 (PP1) through an RVXF motif [PMID:14640981, PMID:16162498]. WBP11 is required for correct splicing of ~200 introns, including introns in TUBGCP6, thereby maintaining centriole duplication and, in cancer contexts, sustaining expression of MCM7 and other targets [PMID:31874114, PMID:38561505]. WBP11 additionally stabilizes NONO protein by competitively blocking its UFMylation at Lys198, linking it to glycolysis regulation [PMID:41184530]. Haploinsufficiency of WBP11 causes VACTERL-spectrum congenital malformations in humans and mice, and homozygous loss is embryonic lethal [PMID:33276377].

XXYLT1 is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, type II membrane-bound UDP-xylose:α-xyloside α1,3-xylosyltransferase that catalyzes the addition of the second (terminal) xylose to the Xylα1-3Glcβ1-O-Ser trisaccharide on EGF repeats of Notch receptors and other proteins, acting downstream of POGLUT1 and GXYLT1/2 in the O-glucosylation pathway [PMID:22117070, PMID:30665188]. Crystal structures capturing the Michaelis complex with natural substrates revealed that XXYLT1 employs an SNi-like retaining catalytic mechanism, with the EGF-repeat acceptor undergoing a large conformational change upon active-site binding that determines substrate specificity, and proper EGF-repeat folding and positively charged residues within the O-glucose consensus sequence are required for efficient catalysis [PMID:26414444, PMID:22872643]. This terminal xylosylation fine-tunes Notch signaling: genetic deletion in Drosophila promotes Delta-mediated Notch activation in sensitized backgrounds, and XXYLT1 knockout in mammalian Jurkat cells enhances NOTCH1 activation without altering receptor surface levels, indicating that XXYLT1-mediated glycosylation acts as a negative modulator of Notch receptor activation [PMID:30169771, PMID:41140820].

Yju2 (human ortholog CCDC94) is an essential pre-mRNA splicing factor that positions the branch-site nucleophile at the spliceosome catalytic center to enable the first transesterification reaction. After Prp2-mediated activation generates the B* complex, Yju2 is recruited via the NTC component Ntc90 and directly contacts U2 snRNA near the branch-point sequence, repositioning the U2/BPS duplex to within ~4 Å of the catalytic metal required for branching [PMID:30879786, PMID:23438600, PMID:19617314]. Following the first catalytic step, the DEAH-box ATPase Prp16 remodels Yju2 binding, releasing it from the active site while allowing it to remain NTC-tethered to promote exon ligation; Fyv6 then occupies the vacated site to facilitate second-step catalysis [PMID:21098140, PMID:33705709, PMID:39688371]. High-resolution cryo-EM structures of the C, C*, and B* complexes have defined the structural basis for Yju2's catalytic role and its ordered displacement during spliceosome remodeling [PMID:27459055, PMID:27980089, PMID:29301961].

YME1L1 is a mitochondrial inner-membrane i-AAA protease that constitutively cleaves OPA1 at the S2 site to balance mitochondrial fusion and fission, and degrades a broad substrate repertoire—including respiratory chain subunits, TIM23 translocase components (TIMM17A via a C-terminal degron), the lipid transfer protein PRELID1, the glycine transporter SLC25A38, and the MICOS subunit MIC13—thereby remodeling the mitochondrial proteome in response to metabolic and stress signals [PMID:17709429, PMID:22262461, PMID:24315374, PMID:31695197, PMID:39774271, PMID:40338741]. It operates within the SLP2–PARL–YME1L (SPY) complex at the inner membrane, is reciprocally regulated with OMA1 under distinct bioenergetic stress conditions, and is allosterically coupled between its AAA+ ATPase and zinc-metalloprotease domains through a conserved salt bridge stabilized by ATP and Zn²⁺ binding [PMID:27737933, PMID:26923599, PMID:32340357]. Its activity is modulated upstream by the mTORC1–LIPIN1–phosphatidylethanolamine signaling axis, Sirt3-mediated deacetylation, and GDF11/Smad2/3 transcriptional input, and its loss in neural stem cells drives irreversible metabolic reprogramming away from fatty acid oxidation [PMID:31695197, PMID:36433732, PMID:32515551, PMID:35172139]. Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in YME1L1 cause a mitochondriopathy with optic nerve atrophy, neurodegeneration, and secondary 3-methylglutaconic aciduria in humans [PMID:27495975, PMID:40255048].

ZCRB1 is a nuclear RNA-binding protein that functions as a core component of the U11/U12 minor spliceosome, where it is recruited to U12 snRNA to ensure proper splicing of U12-type introns; loss of ZCRB1 causes global dysregulation of minor intron splicing, impairing ciliogenesis and activating WNT signaling [PMID:37037902, PMID:39149385]. ZCRB1 contains an N-terminal RNA-binding motif and a CCHC zinc finger domain, localizes to the nucleoplasm, and its RNA-binding activity also promotes Alu element-mediated circular RNA biogenesis [PMID:16959469, PMID:35538499]. Upon coronavirus infection, ZCRB1 translocates from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, associates with viral replicase/transcriptase complexes via binding to the 5′-UTR of viral RNA, and is required for efficient viral RNA synthesis [PMID:22362731]. As a U12-type splicing factor, ZCRB1 controls splicing of specific minor introns such as USP21 intron 11, linking its loss to intron retention and reduced USP21 expression in hepatocellular carcinoma cells [PMID:41258964].

ZNF85 is a KRAB-containing zinc finger transcriptional repressor that localizes to the nucleus via a nuclear localization signal in the spacer region between its KRAB and zinc finger domains [PMID:9839802]. Its zinc finger domain binds DNA in a zinc-dependent manner, while the KRAB(A) domain mediates transcriptional repression that is significantly enhanced by the KRAB(B) domain, with both domains recruiting nuclear cofactor proteins implicated in the repression mechanism [PMID:9839802].
